title: Water Remembers
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 9 of 40
content:
Katara kissed me six days after Aang did.

Not that I was counting.

Toph was counting.

She announced the number at breakfast.

“Six.”

Aang looked up from his fruit. “Six what?”

“Days.”

Katara closed her eyes. “Toph.”

“What? I like statistics now. Paperwork’s been a bad influence.”

I threw a napkin at her.

Toph caught it and wiped her mouth.

The waiting had become its own kind of intimacy.

Katara did not avoid me. If anything, she seemed more deliberate. She touched my hand when she passed me something. Sat close enough that our knees met under tables. Asked whether I wanted to walk home with her after late clinic shifts.

She never used those moments to corner me into the kiss everyone knew was coming.

That made me want it more.

On the sixth day, rain came down hard enough to flood the lower market.

Cranefish Town’s drainage system had improved from “actively hostile” to “merely inadequate,” which meant the southern channel overflowed into three streets and a warehouse courtyard.

By noon I was soaked to the skin.

Katara stood in the middle of the street redirecting water toward the river in broad, controlled sweeps. She worked with two local waterbenders, but the volume was too much for finesse. Brown floodwater rolled around my calves.

“Get the records upstairs!” I shouted to the warehouse staff.

A worker slipped near the loading ramp.

I caught their arm.

The current hit both of us.

For one horrible second my feet left the ground.

The world became water and noise.

Then something wrapped around my waist and yanked me sideways.

A ribbon of clean water.

Katara.

She pulled me onto the steps hard enough that I collided with her.

Her hands gripped my shoulders.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

Her face was furious.

Not at me.

At the possibility.

I touched her wrist. “Katara.”

She breathed once.

Twice.

The anger changed shape.

“Don’t do that again.”

“I’ll schedule future floods more responsibly.”

Her mouth twitched despite herself.

“Go inside.”

“I can help.”

“You can help by not making me rescue you twice.”

“Twice?”

“You count the first day with the wall.”

“That was not water.”

“I’m counting it.”

“Toph is ruining all of you.”

Katara pushed wet hair away from her face. “Inside.”

I obeyed.

Mostly because I knew the difference between care and control now, and because Katara had work to do that would be easier if she was not watching me drown.

The flood receded by evening.

We ended up at the clinic wrapped in borrowed blankets while our clothes dried near the stove. Aang had gone to inspect the upstream gate. Toph was helping stabilize a collapsed retaining wall.

For once, Katara and I were alone.

She sat across from me at the little kitchen table, hair loose around her shoulders.

Without her usual braid and arm wraps, she looked younger.

Not less capable.

Simply tired enough to let the armor loosen.

“You scared me,” she said.

“I know.”

“I hate that.”

“Being scared?”

“Not being able to control what happens to people I love.”

The word love slipped into the room so naturally that neither of us reacted at first.

Then Katara’s eyes widened.

I felt my breath stop.

She did not take it back.

Instead she looked down at her cup.

“I don’t mean…”

My stomach dropped.

Katara frowned. “No. That’s not right. I do mean it.”

I waited.

She drew a slow breath.

“I love you,” she said. “I don’t know exactly what shape it is yet. I know it isn’t the same as what I feel for Aang because nothing is the same as anything else. But I love you.”

The honesty was terrifying.

Not because I did not feel it.

Because I did.

“I think I love you too.”

Katara looked up.

“Think?”

“Don’t make me regret being careful with words.”

Her smile arrived, warm and a little wicked.

“I would never.”

“You absolutely would.”

She stood.

My pulse accelerated.

Katara walked around the table and stopped in front of me.

“May I?”

I knew exactly what she meant.

“Yes.”

Her hand cupped the side of my face.

Katara’s kiss was nothing like Aang’s.

Aang had kissed like joy discovering permission.

Katara kissed like water finding the shape of a shoreline.

Slow first.

Certain.

Her thumb rested below my ear. The other hand settled at my shoulder. She gave me time to meet her, time to pull away, time to decide how close I wanted to be.

I rose from the chair.

That was my answer.

The kiss deepened.

Warmth moved through me despite the damp chill still clinging to my skin. Katara’s breath caught when my hand found her waist. She leaned closer, and for a few seconds there was no flood, no city, no endless stack of reports waiting tomorrow.

Only the quiet sound of rain against the clinic windows.

When we separated, our foreheads stayed together.

Katara laughed softly.

“What?” I whispered.

“I was trying to be patient.”

“You were.”

“For six days.”

I pulled back enough to stare at her.

“You knew Toph was counting?”

“Of course I knew.”

I laughed.

Katara kissed me again, shorter this time.

Then the back door opened.

Toph walked in covered in mud.

She stopped.

Her head tilted.

“Finally.”

Katara picked up a towel and threw it at her.

Toph caught it with one hand.

“Seven minutes late,” she said.

“What does that mean?” I asked.

“I told Aang it would happen before sunset.”

“You bet on us?”

“No money. He’s a monk.”

“I am not taking relationship criticism from someone who still hasn’t kissed anybody,” Katara said.

Toph’s expression vanished.

Silence.

I felt the air change.

Katara immediately softened. “Toph, I didn’t mean—”

“I know.”

Toph rubbed the towel over her hair.

The bravado came back, but I had heard the crack beneath it.

I stood.

“Do you want tea?” I asked.

Toph frowned. “That’s your response?”

“To what?”

Her mouth twitched.

“You’re annoying.”

“Tea?”

“Strong.”

Katara moved toward the kettle.

As she passed Toph, she touched the back of her hand.

Toph turned her palm up.

Their fingers caught for a heartbeat.

Small.

Unannounced.

But real.

Water remembered every shape it touched.

Maybe love did too.

Not by becoming the same shape.

By learning how to move around each person without erasing them.

Aang returned twenty minutes later soaked, cheerful, and carrying three bags of dumplings.

Toph immediately told him he had lost the bet.

Katara denied there had been a bet.

I refused to confirm anything.

Aang looked at my face, looked at Katara, and smiled.

He kissed Katara first.

Then he squeezed my shoulder.

No jealousy.

No performance.

Just recognition.

The four of us ate dumplings at the clinic table while our clothes dried and rain ran harmlessly through the newly cleared channels outside.

My mouth still remembered Katara.

My hand rested close to hers.

Every few minutes, our fingers touched.

Neither of us pretended it was accidental.

The first time Katara let me help in the clinic after that, she gave me the least glamorous task available: washing bandages.

I suspected this was intentional.

“You’re smiling,” she said from the next basin.

“I’m thrilled by linen.”

“You’re terrible at sarcasm.”

“I learned from Toph.”

“That explains it.”

Water curled from Katara’s fingertips, lifting soap from the cloth in clean ribbons. I had to scrub mine by hand. The difference should have been embarrassing. Instead it became companionable—the rhythm of work divided according to what each of us could do.

After a while, Katara said, “You know I don’t need you to become useful enough to earn this.”

My hands stopped under the water.

“This?”

“Us.”

I looked down at the bandage between my palms.

She had done it again: walked directly into a fear I had hidden from myself and then stood there without making a spectacle of finding it.

“I know,” I said.

Katara’s eyebrow rose.

“I am trying to know.”

“That’s different.”

“Yes.”

She bumped her shoulder against mine.

“Good.”

We worked until the basket was empty.

One cloth remained caught beneath the wicker rim. Katara worked it loose with a fingernail and found an old clinic stamp half washed out on the corner.

"That one's done," she said.

"Because of the ink?"

"Because it's fraying. The next patient shouldn't have to trust a bandage I already know will tear."

She folded it separately. I watched the precision of her hands and remembered how, a few hours earlier, she'd been less certain about touching mine.

"I want to ask about Aang," I said.

Katara glanced up. "That sounds ominous."

"It's not. I love him. I'm finding out what loving you means too. I'm ethically non-monogamous, and I prefer polyamory. I don't want either of you to hear that as a demand to feel the same things on the same schedule."

"I already love Aang," she said. "That isn't what frightens me."

"What does?"

"That people will start calling me generous for agreeing to something I chose. As if my feelings are a favor I'm doing for the Avatar."

I made a face. "They could just ask you."

"They could." Her mouth quirked. "You may notice a theme in my day."

She handed me the frayed cloth for the repair pile. Our fingers caught around the edge; neither of us pretended not to notice. I could still taste the tea she'd made after the rain, and I wanted another kiss badly enough that I didn't trust myself to phrase it elegantly.

"I'd like to kiss you when we finish," I said.

"Good," she replied. "I was beginning to think you only came here for laundry."

When we carried the clean cloths inside, she did not take the heavier stack from me automatically. She asked.

I said I had it.

She believed me.

Later, when my arms tired, I asked her to take half.

She did that too.

Water remembered the shape of every container without becoming trapped by any of them. Katara had once told me that was part of its strength.

I was beginning to understand why she loved it.

Katara squeezed my hand before letting go.

“Learning to ask is part of strength too,” she said.

I wanted to argue that she was stealing her own advice from me. Instead, I carried the lighter stack and let her carry the rest.

For once, neither of us made sacrifice into a competition.

Katara smiled like she knew exactly how hard that tiny request had been. She did not praise me for it. Somehow that made it easier to do again.
